nameStory: This tiny spider is named after Nicholas Marcellus Hentz, a 19th-century French-American naturalist who was one of the first serious spider researchers in North America. The genus name Emblyna comes from Greek roots meaning 'to insert' or 'throw in,' possibly referring to how these spiders tuck themselves into small crevices and bark spaces.
description: Emblyna hentzi is a small meshweaver spider that creates distinctive bluish-white, cribellate webs that look like tiny doilies stretched across bark crevices and rock faces. These spiders are quite small, typically measuring only 3-4mm in body length, making them easy to overlook despite their intricate webs. They have compact, somewhat flattened bodies that help them squeeze into tight spaces, with muted brown and gray coloration that blends perfectly with tree bark. Like other meshweavers, they use specialized spinning organs called cribellas to create their characteristic woolly, mesh-like silk.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Look for small, dense mesh webs with a distinctive bluish-white, woolly appearance stretched across bark crevices or small rock gaps - they feel slightly fuzzy or cotton-like compared to regular spider silk

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small spiders with bodies only 3-4mm long - about the size of a peppercorn or small bead

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, somewhat flattened body that appears designed for squeezing into tight bark crevices and small spaces

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Muted brown and gray coloration with subtle patterns that blend seamlessly with tree bark - often appearing almost invisible against their substrate

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Typically found pressed close against bark surfaces or tucked deep into crevices, rarely venturing far from their retreat spaces

habitat: Look for Emblyna hentzi on the bark of mature trees, particularly in mixed hardwood-conifer forests and woodland edges throughout New England. They prefer rough-barked trees like oaks and maples where they can find plenty of small crevices and grooves to build their webs. These spiders are most commonly found at eye level or slightly above on tree trunks, often on the side that receives some morning sun but afternoon shade.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to construct their characteristic mesh webs in bark crevices. Look for fresh, clean webs appearing on tree trunks.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when webs are most visible and well-maintained. Adults are actively hunting and may be seen at the edges of their webs, especially in early morning or evening.
seasonality.fall: Mating occurs and egg sacs may be visible as small, silk-wrapped bundles tucked deep in bark crevices. Webs may appear more tattered as spiders focus on reproduction.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off, but juveniles and egg sacs overwinter in protected bark crevices. Webs become weathered and less visible, often collecting debris.

funFact: The bluish-white silk of meshweaver spiders like Emblyna hentzi is created by thousands of tiny silk threads so fine they're thinner than spider dragline silk - when light hits this 'cribellate' silk just right, it can shimmer with an almost ethereal glow that makes the webs look like they're made of moonbeams.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small bark-dwelling spiders, but the distinctive mesh web is the key identifier - regular orb weavers make circular webs, while cobweb spiders create irregular tangles. Remember: if it looks like a tiny blue-white doily on bark, it's probably a meshweaver.
contextualKnowledge: Meshweaver spiders represent an ancient lineage of web-builders, and their cribellate silk-making ability is considered a primitive trait that most modern spiders have lost. The Dictynidae family name comes from the Greek word for 'net,' reflecting their intricate web-weaving abilities.
compareHints: Since Emblyna hentzi appears to be the only Emblyna species commonly found in New England, compare it with other meshweavers in the Dictynidae family. Other dictynids may have similar mesh webs but are often found in different habitats - some prefer grass or low shrubs rather than tree bark. The bark-specific habitat and the small, flattened body shape help distinguish E. hentzi from its meshweaver relatives.
